headline: Massachusetts directs $1.9 million to expand paid apprenticeship pathways
dek: New GROW awards will help organizations build registered programs with employers across health care, life sciences, manufacturing and other fields, including 27 direct-support apprenticeships backed by UMass Boston.
body: Massachusetts is putting $1.9 million into organizations that help employers create or expand registered apprenticeship programs, a new round of workforce funding the Healey-Driscoll administration says is intended to widen access to paid training and careers. The [Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-2-million-in-apprenticeship-grants-to-expand-access-to-jobs) was issued Oct. 14, with the awards described as Grants for Registered Apprenticeship Opportunities in the Workforce, or GROW grants.

The money is aimed at apprenticeship intermediaries rather than presented as a general scholarship pool. Those organizations work with employers and training partners to design, launch or grow registered programs. In the registered-apprenticeship model, participants receive paid, on-the-job training alongside classroom instruction and can earn an industry-recognized credential. That structure matters for people who cannot afford to leave the workforce for a full-time course of study, while employers get a way to train workers for jobs that are difficult to fill.

The state highlighted one award at the announcement: the University of Massachusetts Boston, acting as an intermediary sponsor for Work, Inc., received $175,500 to support 27 Direct Support Professional apprenticeships for people with disabilities. That example shows how the grant program reaches beyond traditional trades and into human-services occupations. The state release did not provide an individual award table for every recipient, but said the $1.9 million total includes both renewed contracts and new awards.

The program is broader than construction, where most Massachusetts apprentices have traditionally worked. The state Division of Apprentice Standards says it oversees more than 900 registered apprenticeship programs, with expansion underway in manufacturing, life sciences, education and health care. The new grants therefore land as the administration tries to use apprenticeship as a workforce tool in industries that require specialized skills but may not offer a conventional four-year-college route into entry-level work.

For prospective workers, the announcement is an investment in pathways rather than a promise that every resident can immediately claim a grant. Organizations receiving the money still have to build employer partnerships, identify occupations, recruit participants and provide the required training. The state says the GROW awards are supported by the Workforce Investment Trust Fund and the federal State Apprenticeship Expansion Formula program. The [MassBioEd apprenticeship program](https://www.massbioed.org/students-career-seekers/apprenticeships/) offers a concrete example of how an industry partner can combine technical instruction, workplace experience and income support in life-sciences occupations.

The latest round adds to a longer state effort. Massachusetts says the Healey-Driscoll administration has awarded more than $15 million in GROW grants since January 2023. The Division of Apprentice Standards also approved $988,800 in apprenticeship tax credits in 2025 for 50 employers supporting 206 apprentices, according to the announcement. Those figures measure public support and employer participation; they are not a current count of all apprentices working in the state.

State officials are using a statewide Registered Apprenticeship Program tour to promote the opportunities. The schedule begins Oct. 15 at an apprenticeship forum in Cambridge, then includes stops at Pfizer in Andover on Oct. 20, Waltham Public Schools on Oct. 21, and events with IBEW Local 223 and BAYADA Health in Taunton and Foxborough on Oct. 29. The stops are designed to showcase programs in life sciences, education, the building trades and health care, not to announce that all of those employers are receiving a share of this specific grant round.

The practical test will be whether the intermediary awards produce programs that last beyond the announcement and lead to jobs with clear wage progression. The state says it recently lowered the annual fee for registered-apprenticeship sponsors and broadened eligibility for its tax credit to include AI-related credentials, defense manufacturing and additional manufacturing occupations. For Massachusetts residents, the next useful information will be which organizations receive the new GROW contracts, which occupations they serve and when applications open for each apprenticeship.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts awards $1.9 million for apprenticeship expansion
seoDescription: Massachusetts announced $1.9 million in GROW grants to expand paid registered apprenticeships across health care, life sciences, manufacturing and other fields.
sourceName: Massachusetts Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development
